## The AI Will Fill in the Gaps

When your prompt leaves something unspecified, the AI doesn't pause and ask you about it — it makes a choice and keeps going. Most of the time, you won't even notice. But sometimes that silent assumption leads the output in the wrong direction in ways that are hard to spot.

For example:
- You ask for help with a Python function and don't mention that you can't use external libraries. The AI's solution imports a package you're not allowed to use.
- You ask for feedback on your essay and don't mention the word limit. The AI suggests adding three more paragraphs when you're already at the maximum.
- You ask if your argument is strong and only share half your draft. The AI says it looks good — but it's basing that on an incomplete picture.

This page is about getting ahead of that: telling the AI what *not* to assume, flagging what you're uncertain about, and asking it to surface tradeoffs and risks it might otherwise skip.

## How to Tell the AI What Not to Assume

If there's something about your situation that the AI might guess wrong, name it explicitly. Think about what the AI is likely to assume by default — and override anything that doesn't fit.

**Assumptions about your tools or setup:**
> "Don't use any external libraries — I can only use what's built into Python."
>
> "Don't assume I have a database set up. My project stores everything in a local file."
>
> "This is for a web page, but it needs to work without JavaScript."

**Assumptions about your constraints:**
> "Don't suggest adding more content — I'm already at the word limit."
>
> "Don't recommend sources I'd need to pay to access. I can only use free, publicly available ones."
>
> "My school blocks most external websites, so don't suggest tools that require an account."

**Assumptions about your skill level or background:**
> "Don't assume I'm familiar with this concept — explain it from scratch."
>
> "I'm new to Python. If there's a simpler approach, I'd prefer that over the most efficient one."
>
> "I haven't taken statistics yet, so please avoid statistical terminology."

**Assumptions about scope:**
> "Don't rewrite the whole thing — only change the part I described."
>
> "Don't add new sections. I just want to improve what's already there."

The phrase **"don't assume"** is a useful signal. It tells the AI there's a specific way it tends to fill in the blank — and you want to override that.

## How to Flag Uncertainty or Incomplete Information

Sometimes you don't have all the information the AI might need. That's completely normal — just say so. When you name your uncertainty, the AI can work with it rather than pretend it has complete information.

**When you're not sure about your approach:**
> "I'm not sure if this is the right structure for my argument. I'm just trying to get a draft down — let me know if there's a fundamentally better way to organize it."
>
> "I'm not sure if this is the right data structure for what I'm building. I'm open to a different approach if there's a better one."

**When your information is incomplete:**
> "I'm only sharing part of my essay — the introduction and first body paragraph. The rest isn't written yet. Just give me feedback on what I've shared."
>
> "I only have part of the Python script here — the other functions are in a separate file I haven't finished. Work with what I've shown you."

**When you're learning:**
> "I haven't learned about recursion yet, so please don't use it in your solution — I won't be able to follow it."
>
> "I don't fully understand how Python dictionaries work yet, which might be part of why I'm confused. Can you factor that in?"

Flagging uncertainty upfront prevents the AI from giving you a confident-sounding answer built on information it doesn't actually have. It also opens the door to a more honest response — one that acknowledges the gaps rather than papering over them.

## Asking the AI to Surface Tradeoffs or Risks

AI tools tend to give you one answer and present it like it's the obvious, correct choice. But most real decisions involve tradeoffs — things you gain and things you give up. Unless you ask, those often stay hidden.

**To surface tradeoffs:**
> "Are there other ways to do this? What would I be giving up if I chose this approach over the alternatives?"
>
> "What are the pros and cons of this solution?"

**To surface risks:**
> "Are there any downsides to this approach I should know about before I commit to it?"
>
> "If I do it this way, what might break or cause problems later?"

**To surface hidden assumptions in the solution itself:**
> "What is this solution assuming about my data or my users? Are any of those assumptions things I should double-check?"
>
> "Are there edge cases this doesn't handle?"

Getting the AI to think out loud about tradeoffs helps you make a more informed decision — instead of just accepting the first thing it offers because it sounded confident.

## Recognizing When a Prompt Could Lead to Misleading Output

Some prompts, even well-intentioned ones, can push the AI toward responses that sound right but aren't. It's worth knowing the patterns:

- **Asking for certainty on an uncertain topic.** If you ask "what's the best way to structure my essay?" the AI will often give you one confident answer — even when there are several reasonable approaches and the right one depends on your argument. Try "what are a few different ways I could organize this, and what are the tradeoffs?" instead.

- **Framing a question too narrowly.** If you ask "is my thesis statement good?" the AI might say yes — even if the thesis is technically well-written but doesn't actually address the prompt. Try "is my thesis well-written, and does it actually answer the assignment question?"

- **Sharing incomplete information without flagging it.** If you share half your code and ask if the logic is right, the AI might validate it based on what it can see. If you share one paragraph and ask if your argument is strong, the AI can't assess the full picture. Name the gaps: "I'm only sharing this section — the rest isn't written yet."

A useful addition to any complex prompt: *"Let me know if there are parts of this you're uncertain about, or if my question is missing information you'd need to give a reliable answer."* This gives the AI permission to be honest about the limits of what it can tell you.

## The Bigger Picture

Naming assumptions and limits is how you stay in control of the output. The AI isn't going to second-guess itself unless you ask it to — that responsibility sits with you.

This isn't about distrusting the AI. It's about being a thoughtful collaborator. You know things about your project, your constraints, and your goals that the AI doesn't. When you share those, you get better results. When you don't, you get something that looks finished but might have silent problems baked in.
